Aerial Wildlife Survey Report 
Wildlife Management Unit 112 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2021) 
 
Background 
The Lethbridge Wildlife Management Unit 112 (WMU 112) covers an area of 3,797.3 km2 and includes the Chin 
Coulee and Forty Mile Coulee systems. The WMU is almost entirely dry mixed-grass with small portions of mixed-
grass subregion along the west and east edges. Agriculture, including dryland and irrigated farming as well as 
ranching, are the primary land-use in WMU 112. The land is primarily privately owned. 
Hunter harvest in WMU 112 is currently managed using a special licence draw for antlered and antlerless mule 
deer and antlerless white-tailed deer. Antlered and antlerless white-tailed deer and mule deer general archery 
licences are available for purchase. Landowner licences for mule deer are also available to eligible residents. 
A survey for mule deer was last conducted for WMU 112 in 2002 using the random stratified block methodology 
(Random Block) and at that time mule deer abundance was estimated to be 512 individuals (see Table 1 for more 
details on previous ungulate survey estimates). 
The objective of the February 2021 survey was to assess the status of the ungulate population in WMU 112 by 
determining estimates for abundance, density and age-sex composition. Observations were also recorded for 
additional species of game management or conservation concern including elk, pronghorn, carnivores, game birds, 
and sensitive or At Risk species. 
Survey Method 
The transect survey was conducted flying 24 east-west lines at 1.6 km intervals, with 50% coverage (800 m wide 
survey strip) from February 7-10, 2021 for a total survey effort of 2,064 km. Survey conditions were excellent for 
snow cover and good to fair visibility. Observers counted all mule deer, white-tailed deer, moose and elk within 400 
meters of each side of the aircraft (Bell 206 L4). At each observation point, ungulates were classified by species, 
and when possible, sex and age was recorded – though to limit animal stress in extreme cold conditions 
classification of age and sex was limited. Because transects varied in length (see Krebs 2014, Jolly 1969), the 
average density (R; #/km2) of mule deer and white-tailed deer was calculated by summing the total animals 
counted per transect (∑x) by total area searched (length of transects multiplied by 800 m survey strip [∑z]). For a 
population estimate (unequal sized units, sampling without replacement), the average density (R) was multiplied by 
the area of the WMU (Z). The width of the 90% confidence interval was calculated by multiplying the t statistic for 
the left-tailed inverse of the Student’s t-distribution, (t0.05,df = n - 1) by standard error (SE; without replacement) of the 
abundance estimate where SE = sq root variance, and variance = N*(N-n)/(n*(n-1))*(∑x2+R2*∑z2-2*R*∑xz) with N 
as the total number of possible transects given 100% coverage, and n as the number of transects sampled. It was 
assumed that 100% of deer were detected within the 800 m survey strip, based on the sightability found in 
previous deer surveys conducted in the grassland natural region and to provide a conservative estimate of the 
deer population. 
Results 
Mule Deer 
A total of 1,171 mule deer were observed in 67 groups (Table 2). The estimated density was 0.71 mule deer/km2 
(90% CI 0.48 – 0.94) and the estimated abundance was 2,693 individuals (90% CI 1,815 – 3,571; CV = 19.0%). A 
total of 801 mule deer were successfully classified and the buck:doe:fawn ratio was estimated to be 27:100:34.

White-tailed Deer 
A total of 784 white-tailed deer were observed in 43 groups (Table 2). The estimated density was 0.47 deer/km2 
(90% CI 0.34 – 0.61) and the estimated abundance was 1,803 individuals (90% CI 1,294 – 2,312; CV = 16.5%).  
 
A total of seven moose and 504 pronghorn were observed during the survey, though no elk were observed. In 
addition, one short-eared owl, four golden eagles, six bald eagles, 16 sharp-tailed grouse, four red fox, one great 
blue heron rookery, and 158 coyotes were observed.
